speaker: melissamarsh
text: Yes on April the 27th the Michigan Supreme Court issued a decision in the case of DeRuiter versus the township of Byron and held that municipalities may lawfully establish locations where medical marijuana caregivers must be located within a municipality. Prior to this decision the relevant case law in Michigan had been that municipalities could not regulate or dictate where these caregivers could establish a grow operation within the municipality. Thus prior to this recent Michigan Supreme Court decision registered Michigan medical marijuana caregivers could essentially operate from any location they desired in a municipality in the state. Because the Michigan Supreme Court has ruled that municipalities can place limitations on where medical marijuana caregivers can cultivate marijuana within a municipality we are presenting for your consideration a proposed zoning ordinance that restricts the locations of medical marijuana caregiver grows to the already established green zones in the city. The green zone map takes into consideration and is based on maintaining adequate separation distances from these areas including school buildings, churches, family child care homes, group child care homes, and residential districts where residential units are located. This map is identical to the map approved by city council for medical marijuana facilities and is identical to the the map that has been presented to city council in defining where adult use marijuana establishments can be located. In addition the proposed amendment adds several other conditions that must be adhered to by caregivers if they locate to one of the approved parcels. These conditions are consistent with the and complement the medical marijuana act and are thus permissible conditions in the decision of Derrida versus the township of Byron. The planning commission considered this proposed zoning ordinance amendment on May the 27th and conducted the required public hearing on June the 16th. Pursuant to state law city ordinance and charter and the planning commission they moved to recommend that council adopt the proposed zoning ordinance amendment after it held the required public hearing. Should the majority of city council desire to approve this proposed zoning ordinance amendment the appropriate motion would be to adopt ordinance 2158 at first reading and schedule a second reading and public hearing of the proposed zoning ordinance amendment for July the 13th 2020. And so I appreciate that now we are working hard to act on these cries for justice. And I just, I apologize for taking so long, but I am passionate about this. And I think it is something that we just cannot stop. When we see statues and social constructs being struck down, we need to ask ourselves, does this symbol or statue or this song or this logo or this mascot represent oppression and suffering, not for you, but for others? Then it has to go. And so when we learn, we do better. And we do better, not just for ourselves, but we do better for all of us.

speaker: counciwomanky
text: Thank you. Councilwoman Clark. Hi, I got a couple of things. Thank you, everyone, for being here. It's incredible to see the numbers on this grow, grow, grow every week. I hope we're able to provide a live experience once we're indoors, because having so many people involved has been great. I just want to address a couple of people who were able to speak out at public comment tonight. Mr. Josh West, he was an attorney for another client in the marijuana industry. I would love to meet your client in person. We've seen a lot of the people from the medical marijuana industry, the recreational marijuana industry, come out and introduce themselves to our residents and city council. I can't get the gist of who your client is based on his LLC name, so I would love to meet him personally and get an idea for what he's doing. I wasn't on city council when they chose the first licenses and when they picked the process to choose licenses. If I was, I would have loved to see some of these smaller businesses get a crack at it. I spoke with a gentleman named Eric. He's the owner of Toyology Toys in Royal Oak, and he wanted a shot at getting a space too, and he fell in fourth place. I'd love to see the new licensing opportunity open up to maybe some smaller business. He's got a couple of real big players here in the city, so that's kind of where I'm at on that. Megan, I would love to see your tech talk. If you could give us a link, you could post it live in the Facebook feed so people can see it or message it to me personally. I'd love to watch it, and I want to make sure that that our residents are able to get the opportunity to share that too, so if you could pass that along, I would love it. Everyone who came out to speak about the mayoral race, it is very point of contention here on city council. I haven't seen any conversations go on on Facebook, so I had no idea that so many residents knew what was going on inside of the city council, so it's good to know that the conversations are happening out there, and I agree. I don't think that we need a special election. I think that the natural choice would be to move our mayor pro tem, who was voted on by six other members of council to be our stand-in mayor, to sort of take that seat until the next election, and I agree. Mark Bliss could probably win mayor if he ran for mayor, but I'd like to see our residents choose our mayor because that's the mayor that we're going to be with, and I want our residents to pick who it is that they want to represent the leadership in this city, so there are more than one way to avoid a special election, and that would all be for us to support one member of city council. We've had a lot of chaos in this city over the past year, and I am brand new to city council this year, and I got tossed right into the deep end in December, and Rosalynn Grafstein has proved to be a tremendous leader. Even Mayor Hartwell will attest to that, but she did a great job in dealing with electroplating services. She's done a great job working in COVID. She's planting ferns and trees and pollinator plants all over the city. She's helping out with the emergency food pantry, and I see her face literally everywhere I go doing stuff all over the community, so what I would like to see is for all of our city council to support our mayor pro tem, to move into that mayoral seat, and to have a next natural election, pull Bob Bettings back in to fill that vacant seat, and keep the tremendous team dynamic that we've been building over this past year, because I agree we have a great council. I'd love to see it trucking along exactly how it is, because we've made a lot of progress in a very little time. So I also wanted to point out that there's a couple of events happening around the city revolving Black Lives Matter. Micah Cooper, who is a Lamphere High School student, just hosted his first speech rally protest, and there was a couple dozen people there, and him and two of his friends were able to speak their minds about the current climate of the country. I was in tears the entire time. It was one of the most motivational things I've ever seen, and you should have saw these kids' faces light up when they saw the support of the adults and the other children in the room. It was just absolutely amazing. Micah is going to be doing more of these soapbox rallies, soapbox speech rallies throughout town, so please keep an eye out for what he's doing, because he's going places, and he has got passion and heart, and it's just amazing to watch him grow. Madison Heights Sinner Students United and the Madison Heights Anti-Racist Coalition were born from this movement here in our city, and these little communities on Facebook have been growing and growing and growing. Both organizations are working together, along with other local city organizations, to put together a town hall meeting to have a discussion about race, and I have just the details of that information here. So the event is going to be called Courageous Conversations, a town hall on race in Madison Heights. It's sponsored by Madison Heights Citizens United, and you can find them on Facebook. They're already growing very big. It'll be from 6 30 p.m. to 9 p.m. Thursday, July 9th at the Gazebo in front of City Hall, so please join us there. You're encouraged to bring your own seat. Maybe we'll have a contest to see who can bring the most creative seat, and we'll throw the arts board into that too. They're going to have a short discussion by a diverse panel of residents and community leaders, so there are some set leaders to discuss, but they also like to open up a candid discussion forum to hear from the residents about their racial concerns. One of the things these groups is trying to find out is, is there racism in our city? Yes, of course there is. How do we approach it? What legislation in our city prevents equality from amongst our residents, and what are the areas in our city that we can address to help make sure that we fill in the gaps of these disparities in our city, and of course lead by example for our state, and of course our country. So if you would like to be a part of that discussion, Thursday, July 9th, sponsored by Madison Heights Citizens United. It's called Courageous Conversations, a town hall on race and Madison Heights. I'll be sharing this information through my Facebook too, so I appreciate if you see it, you can share it with your friends and family as well. That's all I have for this evening, Mayor Pro Tem Grafton. Thank you, Councilwoman Clark.

speaker: davidsoltis
text: Councilman Soltis. Thank you, Your Honor. First of all, I want to thank Councilor Rohrbach for sharing her story with everybody. That was quite heartfelt and such a tragedy experience. Thank you for that. Also, on a lighter note, I fixed up my bike. I haven't fixed up, rode it in about 10 years, so I went out and changed the inner tube and cleaned it up, and so I went riding. Oh my god, it's like, it's great feelings, like a kid again or something, but so it's great to ride the bike down the streets and then into the parks and in the Nature Center too. And so I want to give a shout out for Councilors Rohrbach and Grafton for the trees, because I'm seeing the trees on the streets getting ready to be planted, and that's a great idea. It's going to look good, so thank you for all that.

speaker: roslyngrafstein
text: And that's about it. Thank you. Thank you. Mr. Soltis, I wish you had gotten your bike ready earlier, because I had surgery a week and a half ago on my foot, and I won't be on my bike for a while, but I would have joined you, so we'll see. So first off, I want to thank everybody who has given me well wishes on my recovery. I've moved from a soft cast to a boot. This, similar to Mr. Corbett, well, maybe not quite as long ago. Mine was about a quarter century ago. I had surgery on my foot, and the doctor said, you're probably going to need something down the road, and there was discussions, and then COVID hit, and so once everything started opening up again, we got a spot, and I was able to have surgery same day as Mr. Corbett. Sent him a picture, and I said, look, we're twins, but I guess it was a little bit different, but we are both right now dealing with our own mobility issues, and I welcome going biking with you once I'm able to, but I don't know when that will be, so don't wait for me. Please enjoy it. There are so many places that you can bike here. I go everywhere. I go shopping, and it's great. What you need to get are these. They're called panniers. They're for the side of your bike. Everyone loves them. People will stop me and ask me about them. They're great, and then I lost one of them, and someone found it, so that was good, but anyway, so yeah, good for you, biking. It's great. I love biking. It just gets you everywhere, and there are so many places that you can bike to here. Mrs. Roebuck, thank you for sharing your story. Please don't apologize and think that you took too long. One of the most important things that we do, all of us on council, is we speak for other people, and sometimes we speak from a personal experience. Sometimes we speak because of an experience from somebody that we know, but we are here to represent everyone, and you had a situation, and you shared it. Do not apologize to that. To me, that was your bias as a woman. Oh no, maybe I better not say something. I don't want to take up space. Absolutely take up space, and share, and let people know. A few years ago when I was on the Parks and Rec board, there was a conversation about, I believe it was crosswalks, and Mick Horner, who's no longer with us, was using a wheelchair, and he made a comment about, I don't remember the exactly what it was, but it was about the slope, and something, and he said, well, it's just me, you know, it doesn't really impact that many people, and I said to him, what I've just said to you, I said, absolutely, you need to advocate for other people. You are advocating. It's not something that I would recognize. It's not something I would realize as an able-bodied person crossing, that there would be this issue. One of the things that I am realizing right now with, that I am realizing right now, because I do have my lack of mobility, is how much I took for granted going for walks, and going for bike rides, and just leaving my house. I have to get down steps to get out of my house. So it's temporary, and I'm grateful for the fact that it is temporary, but we need to recognize everything, and we need to recognize all the bias that we see. I know Megan Futrelli's son. I know who he is, and he is an amazing person. Forget the fact that he's not even 10. You wouldn't know that from talking to him. He's an amazing kid, and not only is he an amazing kid, he's a role model, which I think is amazing, because so often, our role models are white, or they're male, or however it is. One of the issues that I know is going on with the Black community is that they don't have the same role models, you know, and this has been an issue since OJ. OJ Simpson's parents, his mother said to him, you're going to be famous for playing football, or for committing a crime. Well, guess what? It was both, and that's really sad, because there are so many African Americans who should be great role models, and we should talk of more. Dr. Ben Carson comes to mind, obviously Martin Luther King, but Rhys is actually a role model. I was talking to someone at his school who was a hugger, and Rhys is a hugger, and he ran over to me, this other child, and he gave me a big hug, and I said to him, you remind me of Rhys. Do you know who that was? And the look on his face that I was comparing him to Rhys. I know who Rhys is. This was a great thing, and we need to encourage this. We need to encourage this. We need to encourage all of our residents to speak up when we see an injustice, and we need to do that as well. A few years ago, Councilman Soltis had a situation that he wanted us to speak up against an injustice that he saw, and he spoke up. He spoke up, and he said something, and not all of us did, and I'm conflicted on whether or not I should have. I did not support him, and I agreed with him, but I did not support him, and I'm conflicted, and I have been because there's also a fine line that we have to go with, but he spoke up. He saw something, and he said this is an injustice, and I'm going to speak up, and we need people to do that. This event where I saw Rhys, it was at the school, and it was about anti-bullying. It was talking about bullying, and with everything going on right now, and there's so many different terms, and you can't use that term, and you can't use that term, so much of it comes down to bullying. It's okay if we make fun of that person because they are only, and you can fill in the blanks there because they're Native American, because they're African American, because they're gay, because they are different, and it's not okay, and people need to stop bullying, and we need to tell them that. We need to say no. We all need to do that, and we as women need to speak up. We are taught to be quiet, don't say anything, don't make a big fuss. Women are taught with self-defense, if someone is being too handsy, you just want to embarrass them. You just want to do something because they don't want the attention brought to themselves, so a woman's in that situation, someone gets handsy, and don't do that. Don't touch me. She's the one who's made to feel embarrassed. No, it should be him. He shouldn't have been being handsy. I can pretty much guarantee she didn't start with that. She asked him several times. That's what happens with bullies, and we as a community need to stand up. We need to stand up to the bullies. I will get the link for that TED Talk. All right. I will get the link for the TED Talk. I don't know if it's something that we can post on the website, but I will get the link for that. I think it's important that we all recognize our bias, and we all have biases. Everyone does. I'm Jewish. I'm white, so I look white because I am white, but I'm Jewish, and I'm not from here. I'm from Canada, which is next door, and so people say, well, it's not that big a difference, but I notice a lot of little differences that I hadn't noticed when I came here, and whether it's because I'm from Toronto as opposed to Chicago or New York, and I've moved to the metro Detroit area, I don't know, but I notice a lot of little things, and I get told, well, that's just the way it is. Well, that may be the way it is, but that doesn't mean that it's right. It doesn't mean that it's right, so we need to be accepting. If we are going to be an accepting community, if we are going to be a welcome community, if we are going to have people who come here, not everyone who was born here stays here, and not everyone who lives here is from here. If we want to continue to bring people here and have our city grow, have businesses come here, we need to learn to be accepting, so I thank you, everyone, for your comments, and I wish you all a safe and healthy July 4th or whatever holiday you are celebrating. The meeting is adjourned. Thank you. Good night.
